transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, what finally got me to make the appointment is that my concentration has been getting unreliable. I’ll be reviewing a chart at the clinic, or even trying to lay out a watercolor wash at home, and then I realize I’ve read the same line three times. My mind has wandered off to everything that could go wrong, and I just… I’m having trouble staying with what’s in front of me.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot, even when there isn’t an immediate problem in front of you?

Yes. It’s pretty constant, even when nothing has actually happened. My mind keeps going around and around—whether my old patients are being cared for properly, whether the handoff of the practice was financially sound, whether I’m going to become useless once I’m fully retired. I know some of it is probably out of proportion, but it still feels hard to shut off.
Looking back to childhood, were you already someone who had trouble sustaining attention?

I don’t really remember it being like this when I was a kid. This feels more like something that’s become a problem lately. I’ll be looking over a chart or trying to paint, and then I realize I’ve been stuck on the same line because my mind has gone off thinking about what might go wrong.
Did these worries begin after a particular stressful life change?
Yes, I think so. It really started when I began the formal retirement process—about a year and three months ago. That’s when the worrying became much more noticeable.
Have these worries been present most days for more than six months?
Yes, definitely more than six months. It’s been going on since I started the formal retirement process, so about a year and three months now.
Do you feel like the worrying is difficult to control?

Yes. I try to talk myself through it, like I would with a nervous patient, but it doesn’t really stop. One concern turns into another, and before I know it I’m checking emails, going back over notes, or asking the same questions again instead of just letting it go.
Have you been feeling down or depressed?
I’m not really sure I’d call it depressed. I’ve been worried and tense, but I haven’t noticed feeling down in that way.
Do you often feel muscle tension?
I’m not sure. I haven’t really noticed muscle tension specifically. I mean, I get tense in general, but I couldn’t say it shows up as tight muscles or anything clear like that.
Have you been having trouble sleeping?

Yes, most nights. I’ll be tired when I get into bed, but once it’s quiet I start going over things in my head—patient transfers, money details, that kind of thing. And even when I do fall asleep, I’m often up around four or five and don’t feel like I ever really settled.
Are your worries mostly about retirement?

Not just retirement, no. That’s part of it, but my mind keeps circling around all kinds of things—whether my old patients are being looked after, whether the practice handoff makes sense financially, and whether I’ll feel useless once I’m fully out of work. It feels bigger than it should, even to me.
Has this worrying started to interfere with your day-to-day functioning?

Yes, it has. I’ve had to slow down the retirement handoff and even put off parts of it because I keep second-guessing myself. At the clinic I lose time going over decisions again and again. And even things I usually enjoy, like painting or gardening, feel harder to keep up with than they used to.
Aside from retirement, do you find yourself worrying excessively about other areas of life too?

Yes. It’s not only retirement. My mind keeps going around and around about different things—whether my old patients are being looked after properly, whether the handoff of the practice makes financial sense, and whether I’ll feel useless once I’m fully retired. Even I can tell the worry is bigger than it needs to be.
Do you find yourself feeling restless or on edge?
I’m not really sure. I don’t think of myself as pacing around or anything like that. I do feel keyed up at times, but I haven’t paid close attention to whether it’s restlessness exactly.
Do you get tired easily?

Yes, I do. By midafternoon I often feel pretty worn out, and it doesn’t really go away even if I’ve had a quiet morning or try to rest. Simple things like weeding the garden or standing at the easel feel heavier than they used to.
